subject: Archaeology
title: Lucy: The Fossil That Changed Everything
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Lucy: The Fossil That Changed Everything.

hook.text: In 1974, a team in Ethiopia found 40 percent of a skeleton from 3.2 million years ago. They named her Lucy.

buildup.text: Lucy was an Australopithecus afarensis — three and a half feet tall with a small brain but upright legs.

discovery.text: Her knee and pelvis proved she walked upright. Walking came millions of years before big brains evolved.

twist.text: The team celebrated the find while playing 'Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds.' The Beatles song gave her a name.

climax.text: Lucy showed that human evolution did not start with intelligence. It started with standing up.

punchline.text: We walked before we thought. Lucy proved it with her knees.

quiz.question: What did Lucy's skeleton prove about human evolution?
options: Big brains evolved before upright walking
Upright walking came millions of years before big brains
Early hominins could both walk and swing through trees equally well

details.summary: Lucy is a 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus afarensis skeleton discovered in Ethiopia in 1974. Her nearly 40% complete skeleton proved that upright walking evolved long before large brains, revolutionizing our understanding of human evolution.
details.whyItMatters: Lucy overturned the assumption that big brains drove human evolution. She proved bipedalism came first, reshaping the entire timeline and sequence of how our ancestors became human.
takeaways: Her skeleton proved bipedalism preceded brain enlargement
The discovery revolutionized human evolutionary theory

faq.question: Why was Lucy's discovery so important?
faq.answer: Before Lucy, scientists debated whether walking upright or having a big brain came first in human evolution. Lucy had a small, ape-sized brain but walked upright, proving bipedalism evolved millions of years before significant brain growth. This reordered the whole evolutionary narrative.

faq.question: How did Lucy get her name?
faq.answer: The excavation team was celebrating the discovery while playing the Beatles song Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds at camp. The name stuck and made the fossil instantly memorable to the public, helping to popularize paleoanthropology worldwide.
